case_name: Mageswaran a/l S Jayaraman v Possehl Electronics (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
section_title: THE APPLICABLE LAW, BURDEN AND STANDARD OF PROOF
content: The role of the Industrial Court was lucidly explained by His Lordship Raja Azlan Shah CJ (Malaya) (as His Royal Highness then was) in Goon Kwee Phoy v. J & P Coats (M) Bhd [1981] 1 LNS 30; [1981] 1 MLJ 129 (Federal Court) as follows: “Where representations are made and are referred to the Industrial Court for enquiry, it is the duty of the Court to determine whether the termination or dismissal is with or without just cause or excuse. If the employer chooses to give a reason or excuse for the action taken by him, the duty of the Industrial Court will be to enquire whether that reason or excuse has or has not been made out. If it finds as a fact that it has not been proven, then the inevitable conclusion must be that the termination or dismissal was without just cause or excuse. The proper enquiry of the Court is the reason advanced by the employer, and that Court or the High Court cannot go into another reason not relied on by the employer, or find one for him".

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
pdf_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf
section_title: A. The Definition and Right to Retrench
content: The term "retrenchment" was authoritatively defined by the Court of Appeal in William Jacks & Co (M) Sdn Bhd V. S. Balasingam 3 CLJ 235 as: "The discharge of surplus labour or staff by an employer for any reason whatsoever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action.”

case_name: Nik Afiq Farhan bin Nik Hilmi v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
pdf_file: Award_1910-2025_Nik Afiq Farhan Bin Nik Mohd Hilmi.pdf
content: It is undisputed that the Company faced severe financial distress due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Its witnesses (Head of Finance) testified to massive losses and debt. For example, the Company projected that without urgent cost cuts it would incur an additional RM644 million loss in 2021. The audited accounts show Malindo revenue plunged from RM2.52 billion in 2019 to only RM650.5 million in 2020. The Company introduced multiple memoranda (unpaid leave, salary cuts, VSS) from February through October 2020 and did not immediately retrench pilots after the first lockdowns.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
content: In Sistem Televisyen Malaysia Bhd & Anor V. Suzana Zakaria [2005] 1 ILR 853 it was held: - “The learned author, Dunstan Ayadurai, in his book 'Industrial Relations in Malaysia' at p. 121 defined redundancy as follows: Redundancy refers to a surplus of labour and is normally the result of reorganization of the business of an employer; and its consequence is retrenchment, i.e., the termination by the employer of those employees found to be surplus to his requirements after the reorganization. Thus, there must first be redundancy or surplus of labour before there can be retrenchment or termination of the surplus. “In Soonavala's 'The Supreme Court on Industrial Law’ Vol. 11, 2nd Edition at p. 424, the learned author stated: “Retrenchment is a necessary incidence of running an industry, but retrenchment is justified only when due to shrinkage of work, whether permanently or for an indefinite or indeterminate period, there has arisen a surplus in the number of workmen in the employment of a Company. Therefore, when a Company gives notice of retrenchment to its workmen and the dispute arising therefrom is referred to a tribunal, the only question for its decision are (a) whether the retrenchment was justified by the circumstances of the case (b) whether the grounds for the retrenchment given by the Company are true, that is, whether there had in fact occurred a reduction in the business of the Company due to circumstances such as scarcity of raw materials on the availability of which the running of the factory depends, or stoppage of work under the orders of government or changes in the economy which made it impossible to continue the business except at a loss or on meagre profits, and (c) whether the order of retrenchment was motivated by bad faith and a desire to victimize or harass the workmen whom for some ulterior reasons the employer wanted to discharge or dismiss. Additionally, the High Court in Stephen Bong V. FCB (M) Sdn Bhd [1999] CLJ 131; [1999] 1 LNS 131; [1999] 3 MLJ 411 held that: It is settled law now that redundancy does not mean the job or work no longer exist. Redundancy situation may arise where the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind. Hence to justify the retrenchment, there must first be redundancy. To prove redundancy, the company must prove that there is surplus of labour or that the requirement of the job functions of the employee has ceased or has greatly diminished to the extent that the job no longer exists or that the business requires fewer employees of whatever kind resulting from a reorganisation exercise or due to whatever other legitimate reasons”.

case_name: Muralitharan a/l Maniam v Malindo Airways Sdn. Bhd.
section_title: d) Natural Justice and Industrial Harmony
content: This Honourable Court notes as persuasive the ongoing scholarly and comparative literature emphasizing natural justice as a foundational element in labour dispute resolution, even where formal legal duties are balanced against other practicalities. Both judicial practice and industrial relations literature highlight the centrality of the right to be heard, procedural consistency, and an equitable (not arbitrary) selection for retrenchment in fostering workplace stability and legitimacy. This is especially so in the Malaysian industrial context with its hybrid model of industrial pluralism and evolving workforce flexibility.

content: Following the “Whistleblower” email dated 25 October 2022, which linked the Claimant with allegations of financial impropriety, illegal money, mafia activities. The “Whistleblower” email named the perpetrator as the Claimant who owns the business known as Logistic Master Enterprise, the Claimant was called for a Q&A session on 28 October 2022.

case_name: Tamil Selvam a/l Subramaniam v DHL Express (Malaysia) Sdn. Bhd.
content:
It is clear from the confidentiality clause of the employment contract that there are warnings and prohibitions on employee acts and actions that warrant immediate termination for serious misconduct. For clarification, there were four (4) charges leveled against the Claimant as follows: Charge 1 Pursuant to the Companies Commission Malaysia’s records, it is undeniable that you are and/or held yourself out to be, sole proprietor of Logistic Master Enterprise. During Q & A Session, you had admitted, amongst others that Logistic Master is involved in transportation business, a business which is in direct competition to the services provided by DHL, and further failed to declare the same to the Company. You had also made false declaration in the Declaration of Interest document wherein you failed to declare, as annually required to do so, any potential conflict of interest.
This was while you are employed and paid a salary by DHL, and despite company’s policy requiring your exclusivity and fidelity towards the Company. You received no authorisation from DHL to involved with Logistic Master and/or any other business and/or work outside DHL. Your acts/admissions amount to unauthorised breached of your duties and contractual obligations as to exclusivity and fidelity, gross misconduct and failure to adhere to applicable rules and policies pertaining to discipline and work ethics.
Charge 2
From the Companies Commission Malaysia records, Key Master Enterprise (Reg. No: PG0198599-T), it is undisputed that your wife, Gowri A/P Ramiah, your nephew Sathishvaran A/L Ramasamy and your cousin Nanthakumar A/L Ragvan has been proprietors for various time period at Key Master Enterprise. Not only you had failed to declare and/or bring to the Company’s attention your family’s involvement, you had also made false declaration in Declaration of Interest document, wherein you failed to declare any potential conflict of interest with regards to Key Master Enterprise.
Charge 3
During the Q & A Session, you had admitted that you and your wife own a Honda Jazz and BMW car. Further you and/or your family members own about 32 motorcycles which includes a Harley Davidson. Also, you have been frequently travelling overseas. Given your remuneration scale in the Company and your declaration to the Company, it appears to be you are holding properties disproportionate to the known sources of income.
Charge 4 Further during Q&A Session, it was disclosed by you that you have set up TS Master of Martial Arts an entity which is of an income generating business. Non-Disclosure of the same is in clear conflict of DHL’s code of conduct.

section_title: THE TERMINATION OF THE CLAIMANT BY REASON OF REDUNDANCY

Tan Tai Wai, Mak Kin Kung & Wong Khoon Sang [1992] 2 ILR 400, redundancy and the situation that prevails has been stated as follows: - "We are in full agreement with the learned author C.P, Mills on Industrial Disputes Law in Malaysia, that it is settled law that it is up the Company to decide the strength of its staff which it considers necessary for the efficiency in its undertaking and the Court will not interfere unless it is shown that the decision was capricious or without reason or was mala fide or was actuated by victimisation or unfair labour practice."
